newsitem.title: INDIA: Profiles of main Kashmir leaders.
newsitem.headline: Profiles of main Kashmir leaders.

text.p: Following are brief profiles of leaders of major forces in India's Jammu and Kashmir state, where voting started on Saturday in the first local assembly polls since a separatist revolt erupted six years ago.

FAROOQ ABDULLAH - Leader of the main pro-India party, the National Conference, Farooq Abdullah comes from the family which has held sway over Kashmiri politics since the region acceded to India in 1947. His father, Sheikh Abdullah, was a dominant force in the region for half a century, serving first as state prime minister, then later as chief minister before his death in 1982. His son was chief minister in 1982-85 and again from 1987 to 1990 when a separatist rebellion drove him from power. A golf enthusiast, he has been criticised for spending time overseas, especially in London. But polls show the tall, silver-haired 63-year-old is by far the best-known figure in state politics and is widely expected to become chief minister again. A moderate accused by critics of being indecisive, he has advocated the restoration of political autonomy which his party claims New Delhi has gradually usurped since 1952.

SHABIR SHAH - Called the "Nelson Mandela of Kashmir", Shabir Shah has spent more than 20 of his 42 years in Indian jails. Amnesty International has called the leader of the separatist Jammu and Kashmir People's League a prisoner of conscience. Soft-spoken and modest, he advocates continued administrative links between the mostly Moslem Kashmir Valley and both Buddhist Ladakh and Hindu majority Jammu, unlike some of the less secular separatist leaders. He opposes the state assembly elections, calling instead for tripartite talks between India, Pakistan and Kashmiri representatives to resolve the conflict. Last month, he was suspended from the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, which includes some 30 separatist organisations and also opposes the elections, for violating a ban on meeting U.S. ambassador to New Delhi, Frank Wisner. A recent opinion poll published in India's The Week magazine showed Shah was the second most popular leader behind Farooq Abdullah. Abdullah was chosen by 32 percent of respondents, Shah by 20.

OMAR FAROOQ MOULANA - Chairman of the Hurriyat and leader of the Awami Action Committee religious group, he is the head priest of Kashmir's largest mosque, the Jama Masjid in Jammu and Kashmir state's summer capital Srinagar. His father, Moulana Mohammad Farooq, was chief priest of Srinagar until killed by unidentified gunmen in 1990. Dozens of people were killed by security forces during his funeral procession in Srinagar in early 1990, stoking a separatist rebellion. Omar Farooq, 23, is a university student.

ABDUL GANI LONE - A former education minister in Jammu and Kashmir state, he heads the People's Conference separatist group and a senior Hurriyat leader. Member of a landed family, Lone is considered to be the Hurriyat's political strategist. He survived a car bomb which exploded outside his home earlier this year and has been attacked several times by unidentified militants.

SYED ALI SHAH GEELANI - A former state legislator and head of the Jamat-e-Islami separatist group, Geelani, 65, is a hardline member of the Moslem clergy who favours merger with Pakistan. His house in Srinagar has been attacked several times by rockets, grenades and automatic weapons.

YASIN MALIK - A former hardline militant who spent three years in jail, he has guided the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front towards a more moderate stance. Malik, 28, is one of the best-known Hurriyat leaders. Frail-looking and thin, he has undergone heart surgery and undertaken long fasts to protest against Indian rule.

MUFTI MOHAMMAD SAYED - He shot to prominence when, as Indian home (interior) minister in 1989, his daughter Rubiya Sayed was kidnapped by Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF) militants. She was freed 15 days later in exchange for the release of five top JKLK militants. Recently, he quit the leftist Janata Dal to contest the assembly polls under the Congress party banner, strengthening that party's chances in north Kashmir. Both his wife, Nazir, and his other daughter, Mahbooba Sayed, are contesting the elections.
